title: Short Stuff: Necco
summary: Short Stuff episode on Necco wafers, the chalky multicolored roll candy. Josh and Chuck joke about never having tried them and describe the packaging, the flavors (lemon, lime, orange, clove, cinnamon, wintergreen, licorice, chocolate), and the name as an acronym for New England Candy Company. They cover the candy's origins: wafers made on a lozenge machine around 1901 and originally called Hub wafers, claims about Civil War rations versus confirmed World War Two rations, and the company's history. Also discussed: the current owner Spangler, a 2018 sale and 2020 reissue, a survey showing 73 percent of Americans know the candy, price, and alternative uses such as communion practice, poker chips and gingerbread shingles.

segments.title: Opening banter about Necco wafers
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about never having eaten Necco wafers and note the candy's reputation as a grandma candy. They describe the wax roll packaging and the chalky, dusty, multicolored wafers.

segments.title: Flavors and the New England Candy Company name
segments.summary: They list the flavors (lemon, lime, orange, clove, cinnamon, wintergreen, licorice, chocolate) and note the candy is a thinner version of Sweethearts conversation hearts. They explain that Necco stands for New England Candy Company.

segments.title: Origins: lozenge machine and Hub wafers
segments.summary: The wafers date to around 1901 and were made on a lozenge machine invented by a company co-founder. They were first called Hub wafers, or Boston wafers, and predate the company's fame and many well-known candy bars.

segments.title: Military rations: Civil War claim and WWII
segments.summary: The hosts say Necco was included in Civil War rations, though they note historians are unsure of this. The government requisitioned a large share of production for soldiers in World War Two because the candy is portable and does not melt.

segments.title: Spangler ownership, recipe change, and awareness survey
segments.summary: Spangler, a family-run company from Bryan, Ohio, now owns Necco and also makes Circus peanuts. A recipe change led to a 35 percent sales drop and a return to the original recipe. A survey found 73 percent of Americans are familiar with Necco wafers.

segments.title: Price, 2018 sale and 2020 reissue, and alternative uses
segments.summary: Spangler bought Necco in 2018 and the candy went offline before being reissued in 2020. A six-pack costs about $18.50, roughly three dollars a tube. People use the wafers for communion practice, poker chips, and gingerbread house shingles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Short Stuff episode.
